The Philadelphia Fed paper cites it as using whale alerts to measure contagion on crypto returns after Bitcoin whale transactions. The ScienceDirect abstract returned HTTP 403, so the h

Near-zero autocorrelation does not rule out a reversal edge. In the Kitron and Wengrowicz data, lag-one return autocorrelation is near zero on major coins, yet a rule that bets against the sign of the previous 15-minute candle captures most of the effect. The authors write that the signal lives in signs, not magnitudes. A linear autocorrelation test alone can therefore miss it.

On-chain wallet tracking is adversarial. Luo et al. report that bots 'front-run trades, conceal positions, and fabricate sentiment' in meme-coin copy trading, that bundle bots appear in roughly one quarter of projects, and that gradual bundles 'obscure temporal signals and attribution', making them much harder to detect.

Exchange netflow is inflow minus outflow of a coin into or out of labelled exchange wallets (CryptoQuant: 'Exchange Inflow - Outflow = Netflow'). CryptoQuant reads rising inflows as 'mostly a Bearish sign' and rising outflows as 'mostly a Bullish sign'; BIT's glossary (dated 2026-06-03) calls the same relationship 'probabilistic and heavily context-dependent'. CryptoQuant's own support is qualitative: charts that 'roughly well-explain' bullish or bearish sentiment over three years, with no backtest statistics shown.

Nansen's Smart Money netflow endpoint (POST /api/v1/smart-money/netflow) returns rolling net_flow_1h_usd, net_flow_24h_usd, net_flow_7d_usd and net_flow_30d_usd windows that end at request time, plus trader_count, and combines DEX trades with CEX transfers. Per the docs, the most recent 24 hours come from live CEX and DEX activity within minutes, while older hours come from an hourly batch that can lag the chain by up to about an hour. History is a rolling 30 days with no backfill. Stablecoins and native tokens are excluded by default.

Inference to guard against: Nansen's Smart Trader labels are assigned from trailing PnL windows and wallets move in and out of the label, so applying today's labels to historical flows lets future performance choose the wallets (look-ahead bias). Luo et al. (WWW 2026) avoid this in their copy-trading study by selecting wallets only from training-set statistics: t-statistic above 1.645, positive mean return, return standard deviation below 1, and trade count above the training-set 25th percentile.

In the sources reviewed, whale-alert activity is more consistently linked to volatility than to price direction. Misbelief: Funding is positive by construction, so read the excess over the baseline, not the sign. The default interest component is 0.01% per 8 hours, which is 0.03% per day or about 10.95% a year simple on Binance (Hyperliquid's docs quote 11.6% APR). BitMEX reports funding was positive in over 92% of Q3 2025 even while contracts traded at a slight discount to spot. Normalise per 8 hours, subtract the baseline, and compare against a rolling percentile (recommendation).

Misbelief: Do not read a bright band as a price target or a timing signal. CoinGlass calls dense zones 'magnetic zones' that price may gravitate toward. Hyblock lists the magnet reading beside support, resistance and reversal readings. MMT says a map shows where orders sit, not when they trigger, that a cluster can stay untouched indefinitely, and that once clusters are visible, participants may avoid them or target them. The three pages cite no test of the magnet effect.

Misbelief: OI growth is not proof of directional leverage. Each contract has a long and a short, and delta-neutral cash-and-carry (long spot or ETF, short futures) adds futures OI without price exposure. Checkonchain (2024-06-11) argued that CME OI growth matching spot-ETF inflows suggested much of it was hedged. CoinDesk (2024-10-29) shows analysts split: one saw rising net CME shorts as more cash-and-carry, another saw directional ETF inflows. Neither measured the hedged/directional split directly.

Misbelief: A large exchange deposit is not reliably sell intent. CryptoQuant lists three motives for sending coins to an exchange (sell, trade derivatives, use exchange services such as staking, airdrops or IEOs), says part of large inflows are transfers among exchanges explained by arbitrage, says institutional custody moves are mixed into both inflows and outflows, and says inflows to derivatives wallets 'should be interpreted as increased volatility risk' rather than a direction. Presto found venture funds and market makers made up 61% of ETH whale deposits to Binance (538 of 879), 13% of BTC deposits

Open question: Public crypto evidence on how long cross-venue price gaps last is coarser than the equity race studies. Makarov and Schoar (Journal of Financial Economics, 2020) find large, recurrent cross-exchange arbitrage opportunities and tie cross-country gaps to capital controls that limit the movement of arbitrage capital, so persistent gaps are not latency races. A 2025 preprint comparing Binance with Uniswap v2 finds centralized markets typically lead ETH price discovery, with mixed results in high-volatility periods. Neither abstract reports sub-second race durations.

Open question: Cross-sectional use is the untested alternative. Presto ranks many assets by a decay-linear funding difference (24 vs 6 periods) on the top 50 Binance USDⓈ-M assets at 5-minute data, industry-neutralised. It calls the result favourable, but the result table is an image, no transaction costs are modelled, and daily turnover is described as extremely high.

Controversy: The cause of the October 10 cascade is disputed. Binance's January 30, 2026 report says about 75% of the day's liquidations came before the 21:36 UTC index-price deviations in USDe, WBETH and BNSOL, so the macro shock was the main driver. Binance also reports a transfer-subsystem slowdown from 21:18 to 21:51 UTC. Bitcoin.com News and CoinGecko attribute the Binance-only USDe dislocation (about $0.65 on Binance, about $0.99 elsewhere) to Binance pricing off its own thin order books, which revalued Unified Account collateral and set off a second wave of liquidations.

Controversy: The size of Hyperliquid's ADL overshoot is contested, and the framing changed. The revised paper (v3, 2026-02-16) estimates the excess profit lost by profitable traders at $45.0M to $51.7M, equal to roughly $653.6M of positions closed, and says Binance overused ADL more than Hyperliquid. A December 9, 2025 post quoted by Protos asked whether Hyperliquid autodeleveraged '$650m of PNL' it did not have to, 28x the minimum. Hyperliquid's Jeff Yan rejects the analysis and says ADL net made users hundreds of millions of dollars by closing profitable shorts at favorable prices.

Controversy: Aggregator figures for the same event differ. Pre-event futures open interest is cited as $175B falling to $125B in under a day (Amberdata, via CoinShares) and as a record $217B (CoinGecko). The 'over $19B' liquidation total in CoinGecko's account comes from Coinglass.

Controversy: CoinShares states that the officially reported $19B is likely understated, with real losses possibly above $50B, and gives no method. Binance's one-event-per-second liquidation feed is a documented undercount mechanism, but no source reviewed quantifies its effect on the October 10 total.

Controversy: In 2015 London Stock Exchange message data for FTSE 100 stocks, Aquilina, Budish and O'Neill find latency-arbitrage races about once per minute per symbol. The modal race lasts 5 to 10 millionths of a second and races account for about 20% of trading volume. The top 6 firms take over 80% of race wins and losses. The authors estimate a roughly 0.5 basis point tax on trading and about $5 billion a year across global equity markets.

Controversy: Do not quote the equity latency-arbitrage prize as settled: market makers contest it. FIA EPTA (28 European principal trading firms) argues that in most counted races the liquidity provider never tried to cancel its quote. It says counting only races with a cancel attempt cuts the race count by about 70% and leaves 20 to 30% of measured profit. It also objects that the sample is 9 weeks of 2015 LSE data, that the LSE is about 2.6% of global electronic order-book share trading, and that profit is measured against mid-price. FIA's recomputed UK figure is about GBP 13.5 million a year against GBP

Controversy: Liu and Tsyvinski (NBER Working Paper 24877; Bitcoin data 2011-01-01 to 2018-05-31) report time-series momentum in daily and weekly returns. A one-standard-deviation rise in today's Bitcoin return predicts a 0.33% higher next-day return (coefficient 0.06, t-statistic 2.96, R-squared 0.00). A one-standard-deviation rise in this week's return predicts weekly returns that are 3.16%, 3.66%, 3.49% and 1.50% higher over the next four weeks. Ripple is significant at 1 to 5 days. Ethereum is weaker, and its 5-day coefficient is negative.

Controversy: Zaremba et al. (International Review of Financial Analysis, 2021) sort more than 3,600 coins on the previous day's return. Coins with a low previous-day return significantly outperform coins with a high previous-day return. The authors attribute this daily reversal to the illiquidity of most traded coins. The handful of largest, most tradeable coins show daily momentum instead. Begusic and Kostanjcar find a strong momentum effect in the most liquid coins, and Grobys et al. find that momentum appears to be a phenomenon of large-cap coins.

Controversy: Cross-sectional crypto momentum depends on the sample. Grobys and Sapkota (143 coins, 2014 to 2018, monthly) find no evidence of significant momentum payoffs. Grobys et al. (the 30 largest coins by market capitalization, weekly, 2016 to 2023) find an insignificant average payoff of 0.90% per week. Liu et al., as summarized by Grobys et al., report about 3% per week on 1,827 coins to July 2020. Do not carry a momentum premium from one sample or universe to another.
